newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Bo says rappers know Diddley about music.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bo says rappers know Diddley about music.

text.p: A lot of things give Bo Diddley the blues -- like imported Japanese cars and eating food in dimly lighted rooms. But "gangsta" rap really makes his blood boil.

"I hate it. I call it rap-crap," Diddley told Reuters. "I can't seem to get my records played but they'll play all this garbage." At the age of 67, rhythm-and-blues legend Diddley is on the road again to promote his first major-label album in more than 20 years, the aptly titled "A Man Amongst Men."

"I started the mess ... and I can't get no help," he said over a bowl of chili before a concert at the House of Blues in Hollywood. "A lot of cats ain't playing Bo Diddley material because I guess it's too clean. But they'll play all this stuff ... and it's just foolish," he said. "It's giving our teenagers the wrong message. It's bad news, bad news."
Hardcore rap, known as "gangsta" rap, has often been criticised for glamorizing drugs and violence.
TROUBLES NOT NEW FOR DIDDLEY

More than 40 years ago, Diddley was having trouble getting played on the radio for a different reason -- blues great Muddy Waters. "In 1953 and 1954 that's why I couldn't get no work," he said, gesturing toward the jukebox on which a Muddy Waters song was playing. "That's what was going on in every club. The cats would say, 'Can you play that like on the jukebox?' and I said 'No'," Diddley said, laughing. "I couldn't play it, I tried, so I had to develop my own thing."

Diddley was born Ellas Bates in McComb, Mississippi, in 1928. His first instrument was a violin but after years of classical training he picked up the guitar because "I couldn't play blues and rhythms like that on the violin."

He rose to fame in 1955 with his first single, the double-sided hit "Bo Diddley/I'm a Man." His unique guitar playing and rhythm, which became known as the "Bo Diddley beat," influenced generations of rockers from Elvis Presley to The Rolling Stones to Bon Jovi.
Keith Richards and Ron Wood of the Rolling Stones and Richie Sambora of Bon Jovi are just a few of the big-name artists who make guest appearances on Diddley's latest album.
"I'm just different enough for them to want to get mixed up with me to try and figure out what I'm doing," he said.
In February, Diddley received a lifetime achievement award from the Rhythm and Blues Foundation, which he said was the "high point" of his career.
DIDDLEY WORKS WITH POLICE

When Diddley is not playing music on his distinctive rectangular guitar, he likes to help out in his local community in Archer, Florida. A father of five, he is deeply concerned about the direction of children in American society.

"I do a lot of stuff with the police department. I go to the schools and talk to the kids about staying away from drugs and fighting and gangs and try and be constructive and not destructive," he said. One of the songs on his latest album, "Kids Don't Do It," adresses the issue of drugs.

"Kid's don't be using drugs. Stay away from the drug man, don't make your Moma give up on you. Don't take your Mom and Dad's gun to school, try and stay in school," he said. "I'm for real. Right is right and wrong is wrong."

Diddley thinks something can be done about drugs. "They need to stop drugs coming into the country. If they went through everybody's ships like they go through my guitar case when I go to Canada there wouldn't be any drugs getting in here, babe," he said.

Another problem is that parents can't discipline their children, Diddley said. "You tune your kid up a litte bit and he's calling 911 and you might as well pack your bags because you're going to jail."
PRAISES MOM FOR NOT SPARING THE ROD

"The system is protecting Junior when you try to chastise him. My momma kicked my butt 24 hours a day and I'm glad I got them cause if I hadn't have gotten them whoppings I might not have been here now," he said.
Despite decades of success, Diddley is far from rich, something he does not like to discuss in too much detail.
Asked if he had any regrets, he replied: "Not getting paid for what I've done. Getting ripped off by everybody. I'll put it this way, 40 years, a lot of hit records. I'll just put it that way."
About the future, he said: "I'm getting myself straightened out and laying the groundwork to stop. I might do this for another two years. I'm 67 now ... 68, 69, 70, that's enough. Maybe."
